X-Ray by Looplet · defect remediation

Assistant Defect Fixes

All eight defects from the Assistant Surface Review taken one at a time: what was changed, what was run, and the one that is still not fixed. Seven are closed; the eighth is a leak nobody can close from the client side, and it says so. Reviewing the change also turned up a defect it widens — a permission grant answering for a chat that never gave it — fixed here rather than filed.

The register recorded how each defect was established. The column on the right says how the fix is established, and the two are not the same question: a defect can be read out of the source and its fix observed live, or the reverse.

Beyond the register: a leak this change widens, fixed here

Reviewing the diff adversarially turned up a defect the fix makes worse, so it is fixed rather than filed. grantedForChat is one process-global set keyed by tool name alone, and “for this chat” was enforced only by the chat-level actions that clear it. Opening another project is also another chat, and nothing cleared it, so a tool allowed once in one project’s chat ran unasked in a different project’s chat. Pre-existing for the twelve edit tools; this change extends it to navigation, viewer changes, the drafting animation and a metered render. scopeChatGrants(projectId) records which project the grants belong to and clears them when it changes, called from the assistant hook’s job-id effect — the effect whose whole purpose is that the chat identity changed. It is a no-op while the project is unchanged, so a readiness or hydration flip inside one chat cannot silently revoke a decision the user did give.

Established by source reading and two independent review runs, each of which put the claim to a correctness lens and a reproduce lens told to refute it — 4 verdicts, 0 refuted, recorded verbatim in grant-verdicts.json. The cross-project case was not driven live in two projects (§7).

2 · The design decision the whole fix rests on

Three separate places defined “read versus edit”, each independently: EDIT_TOOLS / VIEW_TOOLS in skills.ts; the STATE_CHANGING_TOOL regex in contextBudget.ts:93; and workbenchTools.read / editWithPermission in workbenchStructure.ts:46–63. D5 and D8 are what happens when the permission gate keys off the first of those alone: permissionVerdict returned allowed for any non-edit tool, so navigation, viewer changes, the drafting animation and a metered render all ran unprompted in every mode — including one named “Read only”.

The fix adds a third class rather than moving names between the existing two:

const EFFECTFUL_TOOLS = new Set([
  "navigate_workspace", "show_design_in_model", "hide_designed_model", "control_draftsman", "generate_render_visualisation",
]);
/** True for tools that change live workspace state or spend provider quota without editing the project. */
export const isAssistantEffectfulTool = (name: string) => EFFECTFUL_TOOLS.has(name);
/** Every tool the permission mode must judge before it runs: project edits plus effectful non-edits. */
export const isAssistantGatedTool = (name: string) => isAssistantEditTool(name) || isAssistantEffectfulTool(name);

isAssistantGatedTool is consumed in exactly one place: the permission gate. isAssistantEditTool still drives the other four readers — contextBudget.isStateChangingTool and the three pending-action paths: the packet’s refusal, the runtime’s pre-flight and the edits alias that sets and preserves pendingAction. Edit membership still decides the model’s tool list as well, through EDIT_TOOLS itself, since assistantToolAllowed tests VIEW_TOOLS first and all five are members.

The alternative that was rejected

The obvious cheaper fix was to add these five names to EDIT_TOOLS. It would have left the model’s tool list exactly as it was — assistantToolAllowed (skills.ts:144–145) returns true on VIEW_TOOLS membership before it ever consults EDIT_TOOLS, and all five names are in VIEW_TOOLS as well (skills.ts:101, :104, :111–113) — and it would have gated them, because the gate that had to change keyed on that set and nothing else (permissionVerdict before the change: if (!isAssistantEditTool(toolName)) return "allowed";). What rules it out is that edit membership feeds five readers, and the permission gate is only one of them: the other four all mean writes the project record — the context handover’s state-changing list (contextBudget.ts:95), the packet’s pending-action refusal (workPacket.ts:81), the runtime’s pre-flight (workPacketRuntime.ts:125) and the edits alias that sets and preserves pendingAction (workPacketRuntime.ts:152). Added to the set, a pane move would have entered that bookkeeping (§3) and a render would have been counted as a state change in the handover. The gate needed a wider predicate, not a wider edit set (probe-effectful-class.mjs runs each of these against the shipping modules). The variant that would bite the tool list is the one that also takes them out of VIEW_TOOLS — and that is what was rejected. Read-only mode would have stopped declaring navigate_workspace to the model outright; ask mode would have gone on declaring it, as an edit tool, so the architecture workflow’s first step — documented as a read — would have become a permission card in one mode and unreachable in the other. The suite would have gone green while the product quietly lost a documented workflow. A test now pins the separation: effectful, gated, and not an edit.

The class records this reasoning in the source above it, which is the argument above in the code's own words:

Not project edits, but not reads either: each changes what is on screen, drives the drafting
viewer, or spends metered render quota. The permission mode must govern them too, so the gate
keys off effect rather than off EDIT_TOOLS membership alone (defects D5 and D8).

Deliberately NOT added to EDIT_TOOLS. Edit membership feeds five readers, and the permission gate
is only one of them — the gate reads it through isAssistantGatedTool, below: the other four all mean
"writes the project record" — the context handover's state-changing list
(contextBudget.isStateChangingTool), the packet's pending-action refusal, the runtime's pre-flight,
and the `edits` alias that sets `pendingAction`. Added to the set, a pane move would enter that
bookkeeping and a render would be counted as a state change; nothing an effectful tool returns can
clear a pending action either, since isConfirmedRejection recognises only the two draw tools.
Declaration is not the obstacle — assistantToolAllowed tests VIEW_TOOLS first, and all five are
members. The class exists so the gate can widen without the record changing meaning.

3 · Why the effectful class stays out of the pending-action gate

D5 also complained that the render tool “never trips the stale-outcome gate”. It still does not, on purpose. The gate is a bookkeeping device for durable project mutations:

  • pendingAction is cleared on a tool’s own outcome at exactly one site (workPacketRuntime.ts:172); every post-execution path preserves it, and workPacket.ts:81 then blocks every edit tool until it is reconciled. The one other write that can leave it null is the pre-execution recheck’s restore (workPacketRuntime.ts:158), which runs before the tool does: it undoes the intent :153 had just set — for an edit tool it restores the null workPacket.ts:81 already guarantees was there — and is a no-op for any other tool, so it cannot discard an outcome.
  • isConfirmedRejection (actionOutcome.ts:16–17) recognises only draw_architect_elements and edit_architect_elements. A navigation or render whose result is an error — the path that would set pendingAction if these names were edits, since a refusal at the prompt returns before the bookkeeping (workPacketRuntime.ts:145–150) — could therefore never be cleared by a rejection, and would block all later edits for the life of the packet.

So the fix gives these tools the thing D5 actually needed — the prompt and the mode check — and leaves them out of bookkeeping designed for mutations. A render or a pane move has no project state to reconcile: its outcome is a receipt, and it surfaces as an ordinary tool failure.

The same instrument, opcode for opcode: this scenario is the runner’s own archive of the run above with exactly one op rewritten, the screenshot path, so the only variable between the two readings is the source. {"outcome":"permission-card","cardTitle":"The assistant wants to: Move the workspace","cardSummary":"on the current project","storePending":null,"mode":"ask","working":true,"elapsedMs":9066}

7 · Limits — what is not claimed

D1 is not fixed

No client-side rule can tell an untagged reasoning passage apart from an answer. The strip now handles all three tagged shapes — closed block, unterminated block, orphan closing tag — and leaves a space instead of welding. The one surviving candidate is src/studio/assistant/conversation.ts:129, which emits a tool-calling round’s text as a durable assistant bubble: correct for real model text, and exactly how a leaked passage would become permanent. It is deliberately unchanged. Dropping text from tool-calling rounds would silently discard real messages, and the register’s observation was 1 run in 5, not reproducible on demand. All this change proves about D1 is that the site was left alone.

D2’s observation stays unattributed

The weld sits at a word boundary — so the save has the rightcontext. in run 00-20-23-609Z-qa-live-10-ask-mode-deny — which is consistent with a removed block and is not proof of one. The register’s hedge stands: no archived provider output distinguishes that from the model writing rightcontext as a single word. What is fixed is the mechanism the app controls.

D6’s live half is observed for the path, not for the tool

checkPacketIntegrity now runs before authorize and the composed check after, on a single code path shared by every gated tool, and the ask-mode run above observed that path reaching its prompt. Observing it specifically for review_takeoff_item would mean asking a live model to record a professional approval — the one thing the product forbids and checkProfessionalAction exists to refuse — so it was not attempted. The refusal itself is an unchanged pure function with its own test, and the source order is asserted in workPacket.test.ts.

Three smaller ones

  • The manual has 6 characters of headroom against its 12,000-character ceiling. The builder refuses rather than truncates — composeBrief returns its errors when the brief is over the ceiling (build-assistant-context.mjs:149-156) and main prints them and returns 1 (:228) — so it fails loudly rather than silently, but the next edit to any context/*.md will need to buy space rather than spend it.
  • The grant scope is per project, not per chat inside a project. scopeChatGrants clears the grants when the project changes, in the job-id effect. Clearing on every chat change would also revoke a grant on a reload or a hydration flip inside one chat, which is its own bug. Established by source reading and two independent review runs — four adversarial verdicts, none refuted (grant-verdicts.json) — but not driven live across two projects. Those verdicts are copied in verbatim, so their citations are as their authors wrote them and are not re-resolved against the current tree; the two comment-only corrections since have moved skills.ts five lines.
  • The ask-mode instrument finding is a finding, not an explanation. It is recorded, not inferred, and in four runs: 03-26-10-068Z-qa-defect23b-diag reads outcome:"permission-card" with pending:null, denyButton:true and six rendered rows in the one snapshot 12.1 s after the send, 03-27-24-335Z-qa-defect22c-d8 logs storePending:null beside the card it read from the DOM, and the two ask-mode re-runs of §5 read the same null beside the same card at the committed revision. The card renders from usePermissions(state => state.pending), so the obvious reading is that the eval observes a different module instance than the app — but that was not established, and the probe meant to settle it returned {"permissionsModuleUrls":[],"count":0} — an empty list, inconclusive either way. The runs above therefore read the DOM.

Scope

  • All live work is the browser build on this machine, with the development-server session kept attached while the runs were made. Device scope stays tablet, laptop and desktop; phones are out of scope.
  • The change is checkpointed as three commits on feat/architect-cad-engine, one per concern, staged by explicit path, and pushed: push.out.txt records the remote's own answer for the branch, the same commit this page's tree carries. Nothing is merged or tagged, and LATEST-VERIFIED-BUILD.md is untouched: the gates it requires, native shutdown among them, have not all run. The two comment-only corrections this audit made — the skills.ts docstring quoted in §2 and a rationale comment in skills.test.ts, each giving the same wrong mechanism the prose had — are committed as well, so the working tree matches the revision this page's tree carries and that comparison is now the empty one. No Rust file was touched, and the full suite and the typecheck were re-run on the tree that carries them; check-tree-delta.mjs measures the relation and reads those two files out of the commit rather than out of a working-tree delta.
  • Every owned agent-browser session this work started was closed through the identity-checked cleanup script — the eight defect runs, the page’s own render and verification sessions, and the four committed-revision re-runs — each after its screenshots were taken. Three foreign sessions were listed and left alone. The owned dev server on 127.0.0.1:8085 was stopped through its own identity-checked path once the last run that needed it had finished, so every render after it — including the one that produced the file you are reading — opens this local page and nothing else. The user-facing preview on :8080 was not touched.

Proof for every claim on this page is in this directory, beginning with this page's own file, index.html: code.diff and code.diff.stat.txt, full-test.log, typecheck.log, rust-test.log and grant-verdicts.json, and push.out.txt, the push read back from the remote; the checks, each beside the output it printed — probe-tool-keys.mjs and probe-tool-keys.out.txt, check-d7.mjs and check-d7.out.txt, probe-effectful-class.mjs and probe-effectful-class.out.txt, check-tree-delta.mjs and check-tree-delta.out.txt, check-housekeeping.mjs and check-housekeeping.out.txt, check-page.mjs and check-page.out.txt, check-payloads.mjs and check-payloads.out.txt, and tabulate-runs.mjs with the runner-index.out.txt its stdout is recorded as; inline-shots.mjs, which inlined the screenshots on this page; and README.md. Runner reports, logs and screenshots are under proof/growth/runner/ and proof/growth/2026-09-16-live-assistant-rig/screenshots/. The screenshots on this page are inlined, so the file stands alone; report-*.png record how it rendered.
